interpretation.diagram_classification: cosmological / natural-philosophical (computus and natural science): diagram of the year, the seasons, the cardinal directions and the qualities of the elements
interpretation.interpretation: The diagram is a circular scheme of the year (ANNUS, at the centre) divided into four seasonal segments. Each season is linked to a cardinal direction and to a pair of elemental qualities. Spring (VER) corresponds to the east (ORIENS), with the qualities humidus and calidus. Summer (AESTAS) corresponds to the south (MERIDIES, which I read as the partly legible 'aenioi es'), with calidus and siccus. Autumn (AUTUMNUS) corresponds to the west (OCCIDENS), with siccus and frigidus. Winter (HIEMS) corresponds to the north (SEPTENTRIO), with frigidus and humidus. The coloured arcs (grey-blue, yellow, brown, orange) are the lines that join adjacent seasons through the quality they share, so that each quality spans two neighbouring segments. The result is a quadripartite scheme in which time (the year), space (the directions) and matter (the qualities of the four elements) are tied together. It is consistent with the tradition of Isidore of Seville and Bede, in which the year, the elements, the humours and the winds are set in parallel in a microcosm/macrocosm system. The text under the diagram, 'hic temporalis intellegitur tribulatio', seems to belong to the surrounding manuscript text and does not seem to be part of the diagram itself.
interpretation.evidence: Written in the diagram: 'AN NUS' at the centre; 'UER ORI ENS' at the top; 'AESTAS' and 'CALIDUS' on the right; 'SICCA'/'SICCUS' at the lower right; 'OCCI DENS' and 'AUTUM NUS' at the bottom; 'FRIGIDUS'/'FRIGIDA' at the lower left; 'HIEMPS SEPTEN TRIO' and 'HUMIDUS' on the left and upper left. Visible: a large ring, four main segments, and overlapping coloured arcs that bind adjacent segments. External knowledge: the season–direction–quality pattern (spring: warm and moist; summer: warm and dry; autumn: cold and dry; winter: cold and moist) is a standard medieval scheme. Problems with Step 1: several labels were read with low certainty ('aenioi es', 'SICCUS', 'AUTUM NUS', 'FRIGIDA'). The Step 1 readings of 'CALIDUS' appearing twice and of 'humi dus' beside 'HUMIDUS' look doubtful and may be repetitions or misreadings of the same pair of qualities. Step 1 also records the arcs only as 'connected_to' the outer circle, which understates their role. They link the segments to one another, and the Step 1 descriptions of the arcs' exact paths are approximate. The attribution of each arc colour to a particular quality is not certain.
